name: State of Gong
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Gong in Henan was an ancient Chinese fief situated near modern Gongyi where the Luo River meets the Yellow River. Strategically positioned along the vital riparian corridor leading toward the eastern Zhou capital at Luoyang, the small state guarded fertile agricultural lowlands. The principality preserved its local aristocratic self-government and traditional sacrificial rites until the mid-seventh century BC, when aggressive territorial expansion by neighbouring hegemonies absorbed its lands. \n\n Status: Feudal principality; Capital: Gong Henan; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, ancestor worship; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Lord; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 650 BC

name: State of Gong
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Gong was a historic Chinese principality situated in northern Henan near modern Huixian beneath the Taihang Mountains. Renowned in classical records as the ancestral seat of Count Gongbo He, who oversaw the celebrated Gonghe Regency of the Western Zhou, the state exercised considerable prestige within the royal domain. Although pressured by neighbouring Wey and Zheng throughout the early Spring and Autumn period, Gong sustained its ancestral lineage until territorial consolidation annexed the domain. \n\n Status: Feudal principality; Capital: Gong Luoyang; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, ancestor worship; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Count; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 516 BC

name: State of Guo
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Guo was a minor Chinese feudal principality established on the North China Plain during the Western Zhou dynasty. Governing a compact territory supported by intensive cereal agriculture, the small realm maintained diplomatic ties with surrounding Zhou vassal states. In 670 BC the expanding State of Qi under Duke Huan annexed the territory, bringing an end to the ruling family's independent sovereign control. \n\n Status: Vassal principality; Capital: Sanmenxia; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, ancestor worship; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Lord; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 670 BC; Succeeded by: Qi (state)

name: State of Guzhu
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Guzhu was an ancient kingdom situated in northeastern China around modern Tangshan, bridging the central plains and the northeastern steppe. Founded during the Shang dynasty by the Zi clan and celebrated for the legendary virtuous princes Boyi and Shuqi, the realm commanded a strategic mountain gateway along the Bohai Sea. Weakened by recurring conflicts with nomadic Shanrong tribes, Guzhu was conquered and partitioned in 660 BC by a joint expedition of Qi and Yan forces. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom; Capital: Tangshan; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, ancestor worship; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Marquis; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 660 BC; Succeeded by: Yan (state)

name: State of Hu
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Hu was an early Spring and Autumn Chinese viscountcy ruled by the Gui lineage in south-central Henan. Occupying fertile lands near the Huai river tributaries, the realm governed an agricultural populace and maintained traditional ancestral rites inherited from the Shang era. Its sovereign existence was abruptly extinguished in 763 BC when Duke Wu of Zheng launched a surprise invasion following diplomatic subterfuge and incorporated Hu into the expanding Zheng realm. \n\n Status: Viscountcy; Capital: Hu State; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, ancestor worship; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Viscount; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 763 BC; Succeeded by: Zheng (state)

name: State of Hua
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Hua was a small Chinese vassal principality located in western Henan with its fortified citadel near modern Yanshi. Nestled along the fertile lowlands of the Luo River valley, the realm flourished as a prosperous agricultural and trading hub near the Eastern Zhou royal capital. In 627 BC an expeditionary army from the State of Qin marching toward the central plains seized and destroyed Hua, terminating its long-standing dynastic governance. \n\n Status: Vassal principality; Capital: Hua State; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, ancestor worship; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Earl; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 627 BC; Succeeded by: Qin (state)

name: State of Hui
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Hui was an archaic Chinese feudal realm established in central Henan between modern Xinzheng and Xinmi. Claiming ancestral descent from the legendary figure Zhurong, the principality commanded rich agricultural settlements and strategic defensive positions south of the Yellow River. Following the eastward flight of the Zhou court, Duke Wu of Zheng exploited diplomatic ties and local court intrigue to conquer the state in 769 BC, establishing the core territorial foundation of Zheng. \n\n Status: Feudal principality; Capital: Hui State; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, ancestor worship; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Lord; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 769 BC; Succeeded by: Zheng (state)

name: State of Ji
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Ji was a minor Chinese feudal principality situated in southwestern Shandong that existed as an autonomous dependency of the State of Lu. Governing a compact territory supported by local farming communities, the realm performed tributary obligations while preserving its ancestral lineage. In 721 BC the Lu commander Sikong Wuhai led a military expedition that stormed the walled capital, ending the independent authority of Ji and absorbing its lands directly into Lu. \n\n Status: Feudal principality; Capital: Ji (Ji); Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, ancestor worship; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Lord; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 721 BC; Succeeded by: Lu (state)

name: State of Ji
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Ji in Shandong was a prominent marquisate ruled by the Jiang clan in north-central Shandong, centred at Shouguang. Boasting rich agricultural fields, flourishing salt pans along the Bohai Gulf and fine bronze craftsmanship, the state maintained substantial regional influence during the Western Zhou and early Spring and Autumn eras. A bitter generational feud with neighbouring Qi culminated in 690 BC, when Duke Xiang of Qi conquered the capital, forcing its ruler into exile and annexing the realm. \n\n Status: Marquisate; Capital: Ji (Shandong); Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, ancestor worship; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Marquis; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 690 BC; Succeeded by: Qi (state)

name: State of Jiang
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Jiang was an ancient Chinese principality ruled by the Ying clan in southern Henan, centred in modern Zhengyang County. Established during the Western Zhou period, the realm managed river trade along the Huai basin and maintained diplomatic alliances with neighbouring northern states to counter southern incursions. Despite securing marriage alliances with Qi and diplomatic support from Jin, Jiang was surrounded and annexed by the armies of Chu in 623 BC. \n\n Status: Feudal principality; Capital: Jiang State; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, ancestor worship; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Lord; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 623 BC; Succeeded by: Chu (state)

name: State of Jie
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Jie was an ancient Chinese coastal polity of Dongyi heritage located on the Jiaodong Peninsula near modern Jiaozhou in Shandong. Governing an indigenous populace skilled in fishing, agriculture and salt production, the realm sustained autonomous municipal institutions while engaging in diplomatic exchanges with the central plains states. The lord of Jie famously visited the court of Lu in 631 BC, preserving his realm's regional autonomy through the close of the Spring and Autumn period. \n\n Status: Feudal principality; Capital: Jie State; Common languages: Old Chinese, Dongyi dialects; Religion: Chinese folk religion, ancestor worship; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Lord; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 476 BC; Historical region: Shandong

name: State of Liang
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Liang was an ancient Chinese principality ruled by the Ying clan along the western banks of the Yellow River in modern Hancheng, Shaanxi. Positioned strategically between the expanding domains of Qin and Jin, the state played an active role in regional diplomacy and sheltered exiled princes during Jin succession crises. Overburdened by excessive corvée labour demands imposed by its ruler to construct new fortifications, the populace offered little resistance when Duke Mu of Qin conquered Liang in 641 BC. \n\n Status: Earldom; Capital: Hancheng; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, ancestor worship; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Earl; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 641 BC; Succeeded by: Qin (state)

name: State of Liao
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Liao was an ancient Chinese marquisate established in southeastern Henan near modern Gushi County along the upper Huai River. Tracing its royal lineage back to the legendary Emperor Zhuanxu, the state presided over rich agricultural lands and maintained commercial connections between the northern plains and southern valleys. In 622 BC the forces of the State of Chu campaigned northward and extinguished Liao, annexing the territory directly into the Chu realm. \n\n Status: Marquisate; Capital: Gushi; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, ancestor worship; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Marquis; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 622 BC; Succeeded by: Chu (state)

name: State of Quan
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Quan was an ancient Chinese duchy located along the Han River basin near modern Dangyang in Hubei province. Ruled by descendants of King Wu Ding of the Shang dynasty bearing the royal Zi surname, the state maintained an autonomous agrarian realm boasting distinctive ritual traditions. In 704 BC King Wu of Chu launched a decisive campaign that subjugated Quan, transforming its territory into one of the earliest formally administered counties in Chinese history. \n\n Status: Duchy; Capital: Dangyang; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, ancestor worship; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 704 BC; Succeeded by: Chu (state)

name: State of Ruo
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Ruo was a Chinese viscountcy positioned in the rugged Dan River valley around modern Xichuan, spanning the frontier between Henan and Hubei. Functioning as a strategic buffer state between the aggressive military realms of Qin and Chu, the principality frequently shifted capitals between Upper Ruo and Lower Ruo to evade foreign encirclement. Ruo preserved its local autonomy through astute diplomatic manoeuvring across two centuries before Chu finally absorbed the remaining territory. \n\n Status: Viscountcy; Capital: Xichuan; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, ancestor worship; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Viscount; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 476 BC; Succeeded by: Chu (state)

name: State of Su
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Su was an ancient Chinese baronage established in western Shandong near modern Dongping County. Ruled by the Feng lineage who claimed ancestral descent from the legendary culture hero Fuxi, the state was charged with conducting official sacrificial rites to the deity Taihao and the sacred Ji River. The small agrarian realm preserved its sacred lineage and political independence through the early Spring and Autumn period until being conquered and annexed by Song around 700 BC. \n\n Status: Baronage; Capital: Wenxian; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, ancestor worship; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Baron; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 700 BC; Succeeded by: Song (state)

name: State of Tan
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Tan was an ancient Chinese viscountcy centred at Tancheng in southern Shandong, tracing its royal ancestry to the mythical sovereign Shaohao. Celebrated for its erudite court officials and ancient ritual knowledge, the state famously instructed Confucius on historic bird-based bureaucratic titles during a diplomatic mission to Lu. Tan retained its sovereign status through centuries of regional warfare until the expanding southern maritime empire of Yue annexed the principality in 414 BC. \n\n Status: Viscountcy; Capital: Tancheng; Common languages: Old Chinese, Dongyi dialects; Religion: Chinese folk religion, ancestor worship; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Viscount; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 414 BC; Succeeded by: Yue (state)

name: State of Wu
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Wu was an expansive kingdom situated across the fertile Yangtze River delta in modern Jiangsu and northern Zhejiang, with its primary capital at Gusu. Developing a formidable military apparatus and a fleet of river warships under King Helü and the strategist Sun Tzu, the realm defeated Chu and asserted hegemony over the northern feudal states. Despite its immense military reach, long-running rivalry with neighbouring Yue culminated in a catastrophic siege that ended with Wu's total conquest in 473 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Gusu; Common languages: Old Chinese, Old Yue; Religion: Chinese folk religion, animism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 473 BC; Succeeded by: Yue (state)

name: State of Xi
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Xi was a Chinese marquisate ruled by the noble Ji clan in southern Henan, centred in modern Xi County along the Huai River. Benefiting from productive agricultural estates and strategic roads linking the central plains with the middle Yangtze, the realm participated actively in interstate diplomacy. Entangled in a diplomatic feud involving neighbouring Cai and Chu, the state was invaded and annexed by King Wen of Chu around 684 BC, subsequently becoming a key Chu military base. \n\n Status: Marquisate; Capital: Xi; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, ancestor worship; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Marquis; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 684 BC; Succeeded by: Chu (state)

name: State of Xian
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Xian was a minor Chinese feudal principality established in southern Henan along the upper reaches of the Huai River basin. Relying upon traditional blood ties and mutual defence pacts with neighbouring realms such as Jiang and Huang, the lordship maintained local self-rule against encroaching powers. In 655 BC the military forces of Chu marched against the citadel, exploiting its over-reliance on distant allies to conquer the territory and incorporate Xian into the Chu realm. \n\n Status: Feudal principality; Capital: Xian; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, ancestor worship; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Lord; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Succeeded by: Chu (state)

name: State of Xiang
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Xiang was an ancient Chinese principality situated in southern Shandong near modern Junan County. Claiming ancestral origins dating back to the Xia dynasty and ruled by the Jiang lineage, the realm preserved local religious traditions and commanded a fertile agrarian district. In 721 BC the neighbouring State of Ju launched a sudden assault that overwhelmed the settlement's defences, annexing Xiang and bringing its independent existence to a close. \n\n Status: Feudal principality; Capital: Xiang; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, ancestor worship; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Lord; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 721 BC; Succeeded by: Ju (state)

name: State of Xuqu
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Xuqu was a small Chinese principality ruled by the Feng family along the shores of ancient Lake Dongping in western Shandong. Responsible alongside kinship states for presiding over sacred ancestral sacrifices to Taihao and the River Ji, the settlement held profound ceremonial importance despite its modest military size. After enduring repeated invasions by neighbouring Zhu and receiving temporary military assistance from Lu, the domain was decisively conquered and annexed in 620 BC. \n\n Status: Feudal principality; Capital: Xuqu; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, ancestor worship; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Viscount; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 620 BC; Succeeded by: Lu (state)

name: State of Yang
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Yang was an ancient Chinese marquisate ruled by the noble Ji clan along the Yi River valley in modern Yinan County, Shandong. Enjoying fertile soils and strategic access to coastal trade routes across the eastern peninsula, the principality maintained traditional feudal autonomy during the early Eastern Zhou period. In 660 BC Duke Huan of Qi dispatched an army that forced the surrender of the citadel, relocating its inhabitants and annexing the territory into Qi. \n\n Status: Marquisate; Capital: Yang; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, ancestor worship; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Marquis; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 660 BC; Succeeded by: Qi (state)

name: State of Yong
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Yong was a formidable mountainous kingdom situated across the borders of modern Hubei, Shaanxi and Chongqing. Commanding skilled tribal levies and controlling rich mineral deposits in the Dabashan highlands, the kingdom led a multi-tribal coalition that posed a grave existential threat to the State of Chu. In 611 BC King Zhuang of Chu formed an alliance with Qin and Ba to mount a massive counter-offensive that broke Yong's defences, resulting in the partition of its realm. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Feiqiu; Common languages: Old Chinese, local tribal dialects; Religion: Chinese folk religion, animism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 611 BC; Succeeded by: Chu (state)

name: State of Yu
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Yu was a minor Chinese feudal principality situated in southern Shandong near modern Linyi along the Yi River. Centred on an agricultural basin surrounded by low rolling hills, the state maintained modest civic institutions and adhered to classical Zhou ceremonial practices. In 524 BC troops from the State of Lu launched a swift expedition that captured the walled settlement without prolonged resistance, ending Yu's sovereign governance and incorporating the area into Lu. \n\n Status: Feudal principality; Capital: Yu; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, ancestor worship; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Lord; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 524 BC; Succeeded by: Lu (state)

name: State of Yue
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Yue was an ancient kingdom established by the indigenous Yue peoples south of the Yangtze River, with its historic heartland at Kuaiji in modern Shaoxing. Celebrated for exceptional bronze metallurgy, sword smithing and maritime seamanship, the kingdom rose to military pre-eminence under King Goujian following victory over rival Wu in 473 BC. Yue briefly dominated interstate politics as an acknowledged hegemon before internal dynastic fractures allowed the expanding State of Chu to overrun and partition the realm in 306 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Shaoxing; Common languages: Old Yue, Old Chinese; Religion: Animism, ancestor worship; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 306 BC; Succeeded by: Chu (state)

name: State of Zeng
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Zeng was an influential marquisate ruled by the Ji clan in the strategic Han River corridor around modern Suizhou in northern Hubei. Serving as a royal Zhou military bastion safeguarding vital copper routes from the south, the state attained renown for its extraordinary bronze casting, notably evidenced by the musical chimes of Marquis Yi. Zeng balanced delicate diplomatic autonomy against the rising hegemony of Chu for several centuries before being incorporated into the Chu administrative sphere. \n\n Status: Marquisate; Capital: Zeng; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, ancestor worship; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Marquis; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 476 BC; Succeeded by: Chu (state)

name: State of Zhuan
label: spring and autumn and warring states periods
description: The State of Zhuan was a minor Chinese feudal principality located in southern Shandong near the borders of modern Jiangsu, centred near modern Tancheng. Inhabited by an agrarian populace that sustained native cultural traditions alongside classical Zhou rites, the small realm maintained precarious independence between larger regional neighbours. In 585 BC military forces from the State of Lu marched into the territory and annexed the town, extinguishing Zhuan's dynastic rule. \n\n Status: Feudal principality; Capital: Zhuan; Common languages: Old Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, ancestor worship; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Lord; Historical era: Spring and Autumn period; Disestablished: 585 BC; Succeeded by: Lu (state)

name: Malaka
label: phoenician polities;phoenician polities (outside phoenicia)
description: Malaka was an ancient Phoenician coastal city-state founded around 770 BC along the Mediterranean coast of southern Iberia at the foot of Mount Gibralfaro. Endowed with a well-protected natural harbour and easy access to inland silver and copper deposits, the settlement became a bustling centre for metal smelting, fish processing and purple dye production. The colony maintained an autonomous mercantile government until transitioning into the wider maritime dominion of Carthage during the sixth century BC. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Málaga; Common languages: Phoenician, Punic; Religion: Phoenician polytheism; Government: Oligarchy; Historical era: Antiquity; Succeeded by: Carthaginian Empire; Historical region: Iberia

name: Pithekoussai
label: greek poleis
description: Pithekoussai was an early Greek maritime city-state and emporium established around 770 BC on the volcanic island of Ischia in the Gulf of Naples. Founded by adventurous colonists from Euboea, the settlement served as the pioneer Hellenic outpost in western waters, facilitating trade with Etruscan metalworkers and producing iconic inscribed ceramics such as Nestor's Cup. Following internal discord and volcanic unrest, its leading merchant families relocated to the mainland around 700 BC to establish Cumae. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Lacco Ameno; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Ancient Greek polytheism; Government: Oligarchy; Historical era: Archaic Greece; Disestablished: 701 BC; Succeeded by: Kyme; Historical region: Magna Graecia

name: Sulki
label: phoenician polities;phoenician polities (outside phoenicia)
description: Sulki was a prosperous Phoenician island city-state founded on the sheltered eastern shore of Sant'Antioco off the southwestern coast of Sardinia. Established as a trading gateway to the mineral-rich Iglesiente mountains, the colony conducted extensive maritime commerce in lead and silver while maintaining peaceful mercantile exchanges with indigenous Nuragic communities. Governing its civic affairs under a council of merchant elders, Sulki preserved political autonomy until being incorporated into the Carthaginian empire around 600 BC. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Sant’Antioco; Common languages: Phoenician, Punic; Religion: Phoenician polytheism; Government: Oligarchy; Historical era: Antiquity; Succeeded by: Carthaginian Empire; Historical region: Sardinia

name: Mylai
label: greek poleis
description: Mylai was an ancient Greek city-state situated on a fortified rocky promontory along the northeastern coast of Sicily overlooking the Tyrrhenian Sea. Established by Chalcidian settlers from neighbouring Zancle to protect their agricultural hinterland and monitor coastal navigation, the polis maintained its own civic assemblies and harbour facilities. The community defended its municipal liberties across several centuries of Sicilian warfare until being integrated into the maritime realm of Dionysius I of Syracuse. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Mylai; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Ancient Greek polytheism; Government: Oligarchy; Historical era: Classical Antiquity; Historical region: Sicily

name: Kyzikos
label: greek poleis
description: Kyzikos was an illustrious Greek maritime city-state founded by Milesian settlers on the southern shore of the Propontis along the neck of the Kapidag Peninsula. Endowed with twin natural harbours, the polis commanded trade through the Hellespont and became renowned across the Hellenic world for its high-value electrum staters and tuna fisheries. The city retained proud municipal self-governance and naval prominence until Persian imperial forces under Cyrus the Great annexed the region in 546 BC. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Cyzicus; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Ancient Greek polytheism; Government: Oligarchy; Historical era: Archaic Greece; Currency: Cyzicene stater; Historical region: Anatolia

name: Leontopolis
label: third intermediate period of egypt
description: Leontopolis was a Delta-based royal principality that exercised regional sovereignty in Lower Egypt during the fragmented Third Intermediate Period. Governed by pharaohs of Libyan Meshwesh ancestry who formed the Twenty-third Dynasty, the court ruled from the sacred city of Taremu, honouring the lion deities Maahes and Sekhmet. The dynasty maintained royal administrative titularies and local authority over northern irrigation networks until the Nubian conquest led by Piye unified the Nile Valley under the Twenty-fifth Dynasty. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Leontopolis; Common languages: Egyptian; Religion: Ancient Egyptian religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Twenty-third Dynasty; Ruler title: Pharaoh; Historical era: Third Intermediate Period of Egypt; Disestablished: 715 BC; Succeeded by: Twenty-fifth Dynasty of Egypt

name: Roman Kingdom
description: The Roman Kingdom was the foundational monarchical era of ancient Rome, established according to tradition around 753 BC upon the hills bordering the Tiber River. Governed by a line of elective kings advising with a council of elders in the early Senate, the agrarian state gradually subdued neighbouring Latin and Sabine communities while draining the Forum basin. This regal polity laid the institutional, religious and legal foundations of Roman civilisation before the overthrow of the monarchy established the Roman Republic around 509 BC. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Rome; Common languages: Old Latin; Religion: Archaic Roman religion; Government: Elective monarchy; Ruler title: King; Legislature: Senate, Curiate Assembly; Historical era: Antiquity; Disestablished: 509 BC; Succeeded by: Roman Republic

name: Athenai
label: greek poleis
description: Athenai was a premier Greek city-state that exercised political and cultural leadership across the peninsula of Attica from its fortified Acropolis and civic Agora. Evolving through constitutional reforms spearheaded by Solon and Cleisthenes, the polis established a revolutionary direct democracy underpinned by a formidable citizen navy based at Piraeus. Its civic institutions sustained artistic mastery, philosophical schools and commercial prosperity across multiple historical eras between major Mediterranean conflicts. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Athens; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Ancient Greek polytheism; Government: Direct democracy; Legislature: Boule, Ecclesia; Historical era: Classical Antiquity; Historical region: Attica

name: Aphytis
label: greek poleis
description: Aphytis was an ancient Greek city-state founded by Euboean colonists along the eastern coast of the Pallene peninsula in Chalcidice. Surrounded by fertile vineyards and productive cereal fields, the community prospered through wine export and achieved renown for its sacred sanctuaries dedicated to Dionysus and Zeus Ammon. The polis maintained its own civic assembly and minted distinct bronze and silver coinage until Persian imperial armies campaigned through northern Greece in 480 BC. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Aphytis; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Ancient Greek polytheism; Government: Oligarchy; Historical era: Archaic Greece; Historical region: Chalcidice

name: Asine
label: greek poleis
description: Asine was an ancient maritime city-state situated on a rocky headland overlooking the Messenian Gulf near modern Koroni. Inhabited by a Dryopian populace that preserved distinct communal customs, the settlement engaged in seafaring, coastal fishing and olive cultivation along the southwestern Peloponnese. The polis preserved sovereign municipal autonomy during the late eighth century BC, acting as a regional ally of Sparta during the protracted conflicts of the First Messenian War. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Asini; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Ancient Greek polytheism; Government: Oligarchy; Historical era: Archaic Greece; Historical region: Peloponnese

name: Abakainon
label: greek poleis
description: Abakainon was an ancient Sicel and Greek city-state situated in the mountainous interior of northeastern Sicily near modern Tripi. Overlooking the broad coastal plain between Tyndaris and Mylai, the settlement possessed fertile upland territories that supported cattle breeding and agricultural estates. The community issued distinctive bronze and silver coinage and guarded its municipal autonomy until 396 BC, when Dionysius I of Syracuse stripped its maritime lands to found the colony of Tyndaris. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Tripi; Common languages: Ancient Greek, Sicel; Religion: Ancient Greek polytheism; Government: Oligarchy; Historical era: Classical Antiquity; Disestablished: 396 BC; Succeeded by: Syracuse; Historical region: Sicily

name: Amathus
label: cyprus petty kingdoms
description: Amathus was an ancient royal city-kingdom situated on the southern coast of Cyprus near modern Limassol. Serving as the primary political and cultural bastion of the indigenous Eteocypriot population, the city grew wealthy through maritime trade, grain cultivation and copper smelting. Governed by hereditary monarchs, Amathus maintained a celebrated clifftop sanctuary dedicated to Aphrodite and asserted sovereign island diplomacy before facing tributary subjection under expanding Near Eastern empires. \n\n Status: City-kingdom; Capital: Amathus; Common languages: Eteocypriot, Ancient Greek, Phoenician; Religion: Cypriot polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Historical region: Cyprus

name: Amyros
label: greek poleis
description: Amyros was an ancient Greek city-state situated in the fertile Dotian plain of Magnesia near the shores of Lake Boebeis. Watered by the river of the same name and nestled beneath the slopes of Mount Kissavos, the settlement maintained an agricultural economy centred on grain fields, vineyards and livestock. The community exercised local civic self-government throughout the Archaic and Classical periods while participating in regional Thessalian leagues and coastal maritime exchanges. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Anaktorio; Common languages: Ancient Greek; Religion: Ancient Greek polytheism; Government: Oligarchy; Historical era: Classical Antiquity; Historical region: Thessaly

name: Chytroi
label: cyprus petty kingdoms
description: Chytroi was an ancient inland city-kingdom of Cyprus situated in the northern foothills of the Mesaoria plain near modern Kythrea. Renowned throughout antiquity for its copious perennial freshwater springs, the city governed an exceptionally fertile district celebrated for olive orchards, cereal farming and flour milling. Ruled by independent monarchs, the realm maintained its autonomous royal administration and civic institutions across several centuries during the Cypriot Archaic era. \n\n Status: City-kingdom; Capital: Chytroi; Common languages: Ancient Greek, Arcadocypriot; Religion: Cypriot polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Iron Age; Historical region: Cyprus

name: Etruscan League
label: etruscan polities;pre-roman confederations in italy
description: The Etruscan League was a confederation of twelve autonomous city-states spanning Etruria between the Arno and Tiber rivers in central Italy. United by a shared language, sophisticated metallurgy and common religious rites celebrated annually at the sanctuary of Fanum Voltumnae, the league projected maritime and cultural influence across the Tyrrhenian Sea.
